title: Prolactinoma
subject: Biochemistry & genetics
summary: Prolactinomas are dopamine‑inhibited pituitary adenomas that secrete excess prolactin. Hyperprolactinemia suppresses gonadotropins, causing reproductive dysfunction and galactorrhoea. Management relies on dopamine agonists and monitoring for tumour growth.

sections.p: A prolactinoma is a benign monoclonal tumour of lactotroph cells in the anterior pituitary. It is the commonest functioning pituitary adenoma worldwide, accounting for 40‑50% of all pituitary tumours.
b: Incidence 6–10 per 100 000 per year; higher in women (2:1).
Usually microadenoma (<10 mm) in women, macroadenoma (≥10 mm) in men.

sections.p: Lactotrophs synthesize prolactin from the PRL gene. Prolactin release is tonically inhibited by hypothalamic dopamine acting on D2 receptors.
b: Dopamine ↓ cAMP → ↓ prolactin vesicle exocytosis.
Thyrotropin‑releasing hormone (TRH) and estrogen can stimulate prolactin release.

sections.p: Normal feedback: high serum prolactin activates tuberoinfundibular dopamine neurons, reducing further secretion. Tumour cells lose this feedback, leading to autonomous secretion.
b: Loss of D2‑receptor‑mediated inhibition.
Rarely, mutations in the AIP gene predispose to aggressive tumours.

sections.p: Uncontrolled prolactin secretion suppresses GnRH, causing hypogonadism. Mass effect of macroadenomas may compress the optic chiasm or surrounding structures.
b: Hyperprolactinemia → ↓ LH/FSH → amenorrhoea, infertility, erectile dysfunction.
Macroadenoma → bitemporal hemianopia, headache, visual field loss.

sections.p: Patients present with reproductive symptoms, galactorrhoea, or visual disturbances. In low‑resource settings, diagnosis often relies on clinical clues and basic hormone assays.
b: Women: oligomenorrhoea, galactorrhoea, infertility.
Men: decreased libido, erectile dysfunction, gynecomastia.
Macroadenoma: headache, visual field defects.

t.b: Confirms hyperprolactinemia; >200 ng/mL suggests prolactinoma, >1000 ng/mL suggests macroadenoma.

t.a: MRI of pituitary (or contrast CT if MRI unavailable)

t.b: Detects bitemporal hemianopia indicating chiasmal compression.

sections.p: Focus on endocrine history, menstrual/sexual function, and visual assessment. Remember that many drugs (e.g., antipsychotics, metoclopramide) can mimic prolactinoma.
b: Ask about recent antipsychotic or anti‑emetic use.
Check thyroid function to exclude hypothyroidism‑induced hyperprolactinemia.

sections.p: First‑line therapy is dopamine‑agonist medication; surgery is reserved for resistant macroadenomas or acute visual loss.
b: Cabergoline or bromocriptine – restore dopamine inhibition, lower prolactin, shrink tumour.
Avoid estrogen‑containing contraceptives until prolactin normalises.
If tumour does not shrink or vision worsens, trans‑sphenoidal surgery is indicated.

t.a: Start cabergoline (or bromocriptine if cabergoline unavailable)
t.b: Will lower prolactin and often reduce tumour size.
Women of child‑bearing age need safe prolactin control before conception.

sections.p: Conditions that also raise prolactin or cause similar symptoms.
b: Hypothyroidism – high TRH stimulates prolactin; check TSH.
Drug‑induced hyperprolactinemia – antipsychotics, metoclopramide.
Pituitary stalk interruption syndrome – low dopamine delivery.
Stress or chest wall stimulation can transiently raise prolactin; repeat measurement.
Macroprolactin (large prolactin complexes) may give falsely high immunoassay results; consider polyethylene glycol precipitation if available.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden visual loss or new bitemporal hemianopia
Severe headache with vomiting suggesting intracranial pressure
Acute pituitary apoplexy (sudden severe headache, ophthalmoplegia, altered consciousness)

faq.q: Why do men with prolactinoma often have larger tumours?
faq.a: Men present later because they lack early menstrual clues, so tumours have time to grow before detection.

faq.q: Can a prolactinoma resolve without medication?
faq.a: Rarely; spontaneous remission occurs in <5 % of microadenomas, but monitoring is essential.
Trans‑sphenoidal surgery can cure many macroadenomas, but recurrence rates are higher than with dopamine agonists.

exam: A 28‑year‑old woman presents with oligomenorrhoea and galactorrhoea; prolactin is 850 ng/mL. What is the next diagnostic step and why? — Perform pituitary imaging to differentiate microadenoma from other causes; high prolactin suggests a prolactinoma.

A patient on haloperidol develops amenorrhoea and mild galactorrhoea. How do you distinguish drug‑induced hyperprolactinemia from a prolactinoma? — Review medication history, repeat prolactin after drug withdrawal; if levels fall, drug effect is likely.

During a ward round you encounter a man with visual field loss and a 12 mm pituitary lesion on CT. What immediate management is required? — Start high‑dose dopamine agonist and arrange urgent ophthalmology; if vision deteriorates, prepare for surgical decompression.
Explain why dopamine agonists are preferred over surgery for most prolactinomas. — They normalize prolactin, shrink tumours, avoid surgical risks, and have high long‑term remission rates.

A pregnant woman is found to have a known prolactinoma. How should treatment be adjusted? — Continue low‑dose cabergoline if tumour is large or symptomatic; otherwise monitor closely, as most microadenomas remain stable.

What laboratory pitfall can give a falsely elevated prolactin and how would you confirm the true level? — Macroprolactin can cause spurious elevation; perform polyethylene glycol precipitation or use a different assay.
List three non‑pituitary causes of hyperprolactinemia that must be excluded before labeling a tumour. — Hypothyroidism, renal failure, drug‑induced (e.g., antipsychotics).

A patient with a prolactinoma develops sudden severe headache and ophthalmoplegia. What complication is this and what is the emergency treatment? — Pituitary apoplexy; give high‑dose IV steroids and arrange urgent neurosurgical decompression.
